rows.evidence: Q1: Sect. 2-3, Tables 1-2 - the authors apply their own ASTER/Landsat imagery, in-situ sun-photometer and spectro-radiometer readings, a wireless sensor network and WaterWare model runs to a pilot area near Mandria, Paphos, and report ETc values for seven image dates in 2007-2008.
rows.notes: The study is a pilot demonstration of estimating crop evapotranspiration from satellite data (FAO Penman-Monteith adapted to imagery) and comparing it with WaterWare ETc estimates (Table 2). It does not report any result of its own on water policy, scarcity, climate change or allocation among competing demands: the WaterWare optimization of competing uses is described in the methodology but no allocation results are reported, and the conclusions only state that the integration 'can provide scientific data to policy makers'. The study therefore supports only a precondition of the claim (remote-sensing-based ETc/irrigation-demand monitoring), not the claimed policy effect of confronting scarcity, climate change and competing demands. Only one site, one year of images, mostly a single crop (alfalfa/early vegetables); no triangulation beyond comparing two model estimates; Table 1 gives min/max ETc per image but this is spatial range over pixels, not dispersion of a claimed policy effect.

notes: Short conference-style paper (Adv. Geosci. 2011). Full text appears complete, though equation 1 and figure captions are garbled by layout extraction. Results are limited to ETc tables and a qualitative comparison of two estimation methods; no results of the water allocation optimization are presented.
